title: The Trinity: A Bible Study on Knowing God
subtitle: A five-session study on the God who is three-in-one, and the life that knowing him makes possible.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult classes and individuals who have studied God for years and quietly suspect they've never met him, and for anyone who came to church looking for something to believe and found a doctrine called the Trinity that sounded like a math problem no one could solve. It walks through the oldest confession the church holds, that the one God is eternally three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and asks the question underneath all theology: was the point ever just to be right about God, or to know him?

The first session takes up the difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and the danger of theology that never becomes prayer. The second states the doctrine of the Trinity carefully and historically, not as a puzzle to crack but as the reason God can be called love. The third meets the Father who runs toward the returning child. The fourth looks at the Son, "the exact imprint" of God's nature, in whom the God who could have stayed unknown made himself known. And the fifth turns to the Spirit, who doesn't leave us studying God from across a room but draws us into the love the Father and the Son have always shared.

This study won't hand anyone a diagram of God to file away, and no leader should try. The Trinity isn't a problem to be solved. It's the name of the God who saves us, and Jesus said that knowing him is eternal life. Some in the room have spent years gathering facts about God and have never been sure they were known by him. I'm writing from inside that same long walk, from knowing about God toward knowing him.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: Knowing vs. Knowing About
sessions.aim: To begin not with the doctrine of God but with the question underneath it, whether the point of theology was ever to be right about God or to know him, and to face plainly that a person can master the facts about God for a lifetime and never meet him, without either despising study or mistaking study for the thing itself.
sessions.summary:
Most of us assume that to know God is to know a great deal about him. So we read and study and collect, and we measure our nearness to God by how much we've gathered. The first question of this study is whether that's true. J. I. Packer built his book Knowing God (1973) on the difference between knowing about a person and knowing the person, the difference between reading someone's biography and sitting across a table from them.

There's a fair worry here. A study that opens by warning against head knowledge can sound like permission to be lazy, a way of calling ignorance humility. That danger is real, and this study won't look down on the reading and thinking that have brought many people to faith. The warning isn't against knowing much. It's against stopping there. You can know that God is sovereign and never once rest in it. You can define his attributes and never speak to the One who has them.

Theology that never becomes prayer has missed its own purpose, which was never information about God but knowing him. Jesus said it plainly: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3).

keyScripture.why: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3). Jesus defines eternal life not as a place secured or a doctrine affirmed but as knowing God himself, which makes knowing him, not information about him, the heart of salvation and the aim of all theology.

discussion.q: When you try to judge how close you are to God, what do you actually look at: how much you know, how you feel, how you behave, or something else?
discussion.behind: Find out the working definition before you teach anything. Most of us measure nearness to God by knowledge, feeling or performance without ever examining the measure. You're only bringing the assumption into view so the room can sense that knowing God might be something else. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Think of someone you know a lot about but have never met, and someone you know well but couldn't write much about. What's the difference between those two kinds of knowing?
discussion.behind: Let people feel the distinction in an ordinary human case first: the public figure you can't reach, the friend you can't summarize. When the same distinction is applied to God, it will land as something they already understand rather than a theological trick.

discussion.q: Where has studying God been a real gift to you? Has it ever become a substitute for actually coming to him?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves, because this session doesn't despise the mind. You're not trying to make anyone feel guilty for studying. You're looking for the point where good study quietly became a stopping place instead of a road. Affirm the learning first, then press gently.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 8:1-3. Is there a truth about God you could defend in an argument but have never let reach the part of you that's afraid or grieving?
discussion.behind: Paul says knowledge "puffs up" and that what matters is being "known by God." Most of us hold doctrines we've never let reach the place that needs them. Ask people to recognize it, not to give details, and handle it tenderly.

discussion.q: Have you ever been able to say true things about God while feeling you didn't know him at all? What did you do with that?
discussion.behind: Bring each person, yourself included, into the gap between knowing about God and knowing him, because that gap is where this study means to work. You're not looking for dramatic confession. Answer first, briefly and plainly, and keep it gentle.

objections.objection: A study that opens by warning against head knowledge is giving people permission to be lazy. You're dressing up ignorance as humility and telling people they don't need to think hard about God, which is the excuse the shallow have always wanted.
objections.response: There's more truth in this than you might expect, and the study agrees with it. It won't look down on the mind. The warning isn't against knowing much about God. It's against mistaking knowing about him for knowing him. A person can master God's attributes and define every term correctly and never once have spoken to the One those words describe, the way someone could memorize a woman's biography and never meet her. That isn't a call to read less. If anything, it's a call to read better and let study turn into prayer. J. I. Packer wrote one of the most careful popular books on the doctrine of God, and the whole point of his rigor was that we would come to know God and not merely know about him. The warning isn't against the intellect. It's the intellect refusing to stop short of its own purpose.

objections.objection: If knowing God is personal acquaintance and not just information, how is that different from people who follow their feelings and call it God? You're making knowing God sound like an experience, and experiences lie.
objections.response: That's fair, and the study guards against exactly this, because a God known only by feeling gets remade every time the feeling changes. Knowing God isn't warm experience set against cold fact. It's both, in the right order. You can't know a person you know nothing true about, so the facts aren't optional. They're what the relationship is made of: the actual truth about the actual God revealed in Scripture. But the facts were never the destination. They're the way in. Think about how you come to know anyone. You start with true things, a name, a history, a character, and those true things become the way you come to know a person rather than a profile. The danger isn't knowing too many true things about God. It's collecting them and never letting them carry us to him. Feeling, if it comes, follows the truth. It never replaces it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If knowing God is as different from knowing about him as reading someone's biography is from being known by them, which have you mostly been doing? How long has it been since you came to him rather than studied him?
sessions.practice: This week, take one true thing you already know about God, that he's good, that he forgives, that he's near, and instead of studying it, pray it. Each day, say that one truth back to God as something said to him, not a definition. Tell him you know it and ask him to make it real to you, not only true. Don't add new facts this week. Take the ones you have and carry them from your head to the One they're about. At the end of the week, write down whether saying a known truth to God felt different from holding it as information.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, some of us have studied you for years and aren't sure we've met you. We've collected true things and filed them away, and called the filing a relationship. Forgive us for stopping at knowing about you when you offered us yourself. We don't despise learning. You gave us minds, and we'll use them. But we confess we've let learning become a place to hide from the One it was always about. Take the truths we already hold and make them prayer. And to those of us who can describe you and have never rested in you, give what we can't make for ourselves: not more about you, but you. In the name of Jesus, who came so that we might know you. Amen.
reflection: What have I been measuring when I measure my nearness to God? Is it knowing him, or only knowing about him?
Is there a truth about God I could defend in an argument but have never let reach the part of me that's afraid, ashamed or grieving?
If the whole point of theology was knowing God and not just information, what would change about how I read, study and pray this week?
sessions.teaching:
Let me start with an assumption almost all of us carry without examining it: to know God is to know a great deal about him. We come by it honestly. We're told the faith has content, that it matters what's true, that we should study, and all of that is right. I won't take a word of it back. So we read and collect. We learn the attributes and the arguments and the doctrines, and somewhere along the way we begin to measure our nearness to God by the size of the pile, as though the way to God were a stack of true sentences and the tallest stack stood closest. Before we say a word about the Trinity, I want to ask whether that's true.

Because there's a difference, and once you see it you can't stop seeing it, between knowing about a person and knowing the person. J. I. Packer built his book Knowing God, published in 1973, on exactly this distinction. I can know a great deal about a man, where he was born, what he's done, what he thinks, and never have met him. I can close his biography knowing facts he's forgotten himself, and if he walked into the room, I wouldn't know him and he wouldn't know me. And I can know a friend whose life story I couldn't write, because I've sat across the table from her, because she knows my name. Between us there's not just information but acquaintance. That gap is where this study lives, and a lot of our religion lives on the wrong side of it.

A worry comes up right away, and it's a fair one. A study that opens by warning against head knowledge can sound like an excuse to read less, to call ignorance humility and the refusal to think hard a kind of maturity. I grant that danger without hesitation. Reading and thinking and the slow work of being convinced have brought many people to faith, often against their own resistance, and I won't belittle that. The warning isn't against knowing much about God. It's against stopping there, against the assumption that once you have the facts you have the thing, when the facts were always the door. Packer's book is hundreds of pages of careful theology, and his whole point was that we would come to know God and not merely know about him.

Here's what the problem looks like. You can know that God is sovereign and never once have rested in that on a night when everything was falling apart. You can list his attributes and never have spoken, in prayer, to the One who has them. You can hold a doctrine of grace precise enough to defend in a seminar and never have let it reach the part of you that's still ashamed of something you did twenty years ago. The truth sits in the head, correct and cold, and the part of you that actually needed it, the frightened part, the grieving part, the part that lies awake, never hears the news. Many people who teach the faith know this from the inside. They've taught true things about God on mornings when God himself felt far away. If you've lived in that gap, you aren't a bad Christian. You're most Christians, most of the time, and this study is for you.

Scripture keeps pointing past information to knowing. Through Jeremiah, God says, "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom... but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jeremiah 9:23-24). Paul, who knew as much about God as anyone of his day, wrote, "I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). And he warned the Corinthians that "'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up," adding, "if anyone loves God, he is known by God" (1 Corinthians 8:1, 3).

So here's where this first session lands. Theology that never becomes prayer has missed its own purpose. The reason to know that God is good is so you'll rest in his goodness. The reason to learn that he forgives is so you'll come to him forgiven. And the reason to study the Trinity, which is where we're headed, isn't to win an argument about the nature of God but to be drawn into the life of the God who is, forever, a communion of love. Jesus put it as plainly as it can be put: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17:3). Not that they know about you. That they know you.

Over the next four sessions we'll take up the highest and hardest doctrine the church confesses, the one God in three persons. We won't be solving a puzzle or stacking up more impressive sentences. We'll be walking, slowly, from knowing about God toward knowing him, and the test of each session won't be whether you can define the Trinity, but whether the God we're studying has become, even a little, the God you speak to. Knowing about him isn't the enemy. It's the road. But a road you never walk is only a line on a map.

scriptureStudy.note: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." Jesus defines eternal life as knowing God himself, not as information held or a place secured.
"Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me." God ranks knowing him above wisdom, might and riches, the only boast that holds.
"I count everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord." Paul, who knew more about God than almost anyone, treats it all as loss next to knowing Christ.

"For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings." God wants to be known more than he wants to be served at a distance, which exposes a religion that performs for God without coming to him.
"'Knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up... But if anyone loves God, he is known by God." Paul warns that knowledge alone inflates, and he puts the real thing in being known by God.

"On that day many will say to me, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name...?' And then will I declare to them, 'I never knew you.'" The terrible word isn't that they knew too little about God but that he didn't know them.

"But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God." Paul corrects himself mid-sentence. The deeper truth isn't our knowing of God but his knowing of us, a relationship that starts with him.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at how old this distinction is. It's older and more careful than our modern split between head and heart. John Calvin, early in the 1559 edition of his Institutes (1.2.1), says that God isn't properly known where there's no piety, and he defines piety as reverence joined with love of God. On his account, knowledge of God that leaves the knower unmoved isn't really knowledge of God at all. Set that beside the modern ideal of detached, neutral knowledge, the idea that to know something truly you have to hold it at arm's length and feel nothing. Ask whether that posture, useful as it is for studying rocks, can ever reach a person.

Then weigh Packer's own framing in Knowing God: the test of whether you know God isn't how much you can say about him, but whether what you know has turned into praise, trust and prayer. And read the opening of Augustine's Confessions, where he tells God that our heart is restless until it rests in him. The human mind wasn't made only to grasp God as an object, but to come to rest in him.

The discipline is to hold knowledge and knowing together without collapsing either: refusing a dead orthodoxy that knows everything about God and says nothing to him, and refusing an empty experience that feels a great deal and knows nothing true.

sessions.title: One God, Three Persons
sessions.aim: To state the doctrine of the Trinity carefully and historically, not as a riddle to be solved but as the church's confession of the God who is, and to see that God can be called love because he was never alone, holding the doctrine as something received and confessed rather than something up for a vote.
sessions.summary:
We come to the Trinity as if to a math problem. One plus one plus one equals one doesn't seem right, so either Christians can't count or they're hiding something. The first question is whether the Trinity was ever that kind of thing at all.

The objection deserves its full strength: the doctrine is incoherent, a late invention laid on the simple faith of Jesus by councils centuries later, three gods smuggled in under one name. It's true that the Trinity can't be drawn on a whiteboard, and that the precise language came later, at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381. But the doctrine wasn't invented to complicate God. The church was driven to it because it refused to give up either of two things: that there is one God, and that Jesus and the Spirit are that God. The councils didn't vote God into being three. They drew a fence around a mystery the church had been worshiping from the start.

And here's the heart of it. "God is love" (1 John 4:8). If God were alone for all eternity before he made anything, love would be something he took up only after creation. But the God who is eternally Father, Son and Spirit was never alone. Love isn't only something God does. It's what he is.

keyScripture.why: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). One name, singular, and three persons within it. Jesus holds the oneness and the threeness together before any council ever met.

discussion.q: How has the Trinity sat with you over the years: a math problem you couldn't solve, a doctrine you accept but don't understand, or something you've actually worshiped?
discussion.behind: Most people's real relationship with this doctrine is quiet bafflement or polite avoidance. Let the room admit that. You're making space for the session to turn the Trinity from a puzzle into a confession.

discussion.q: The early church refused to give up two things: that there is one God, and that Jesus and the Spirit are that God. Which would be easier to drop to make the math simpler, and what would be lost?
discussion.behind: Help the room feel the pressure the early church felt. Nearly every early error relieved the tension by dropping one side. The doctrine isn't arbitrary complexity. It's the only shape that keeps both truths, and each shortcut has a cost.

discussion.q: If a creed is more like a fence around a mystery than a full explanation of it, how does that change what you expect of yourself in understanding the Trinity?
discussion.behind: The creeds mostly mark boundaries, saying not this and not that, rather than mapping the inside. Free people from thinking they've failed because they can't fully comprehend the Trinity. The church never claimed to.

discussion.q: Read 1 John 4:7-12. If God had been alone before creation, whom would he have loved? What changes, for God and for you, if love is what God has always been?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge of the session. Help the room feel the difference between a solitary God who starts loving after he makes someone and a God who is love because he has always been a communion. We aren't loved as an afterthought of a lonely God, and that steadies people.

discussion.q: Have you ever held a true thing about God mainly as a position to defend rather than a Person to love?
discussion.behind: Go first. It's possible to defend the Trinity for years without worshiping the God being defended. This ties back to session one: being right about God isn't the same as knowing him.

objections.objection: The Trinity is incoherent. One God in three persons is one plus one plus one equals one, which is nonsense. And it was invented by councils centuries after Jesus, who believed in one God. You've smuggled three gods in under one name.
objections.response: Two things in this are true, and the answer is stronger for granting them. The Trinity can't be drawn on a whiteboard, and every neat picture of it turns out wrong. And the formal language did come later, at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381. But the councils didn't invent the Trinity. They were driven to it by what they wouldn't give up. Israel had confessed one God at great cost, and the church wouldn't let that go. Yet the same church found itself worshiping Jesus, who said "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), forgave sins, and received worship. And it knew the Spirit as God, not as a force. It couldn't drop the oneness, and it couldn't drop the deity of the Son and the Spirit. The doctrine is the refusal to deny either. As for the arithmetic, God isn't three of the same thing he is one of. He's one in being and three in persons. That isn't a contradiction. It's not three gods. It's the one God who is, in his depths, a fellowship.

objections.objection: Even if it isn't three gods, the Trinity is impossible to understand, so why does it matter? Give me a God I can pray to. Whether God is one person or three has nothing to do with my life.
objections.response: It may be the most practical thing in this study. If God were a single, solitary person, alone before he made the world, then before there was anything to love, God didn't love, because there was no one there. Love would be something he took up after creation, something he does but not something he is. But Scripture says "God is love" (1 John 4:8). That can only be true if God was never alone, if within the one God there has always been a giving and receiving of love, the Father loving the Son in the Spirit before any creature existed. And that changes your life. You weren't made by a lonely God who needed someone, and you aren't loved as the cure for his solitude. You're invited into a love that was already full before you existed. A solitary god would need you. The triune God can simply love you, because he was never short of love.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the God who made you was never lonely and never short of love, he made you out of overflow, not need. What would it mean to stop treating God as someone you have to keep satisfied, and start receiving from a love that was always full?
sessions.practice: This week, pray to the Trinity on purpose, which most of us rarely do. Each day, pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, naming all three, not as a formula but as a deliberate way of speaking to the God who is three in one. Notice what you usually default to, a vague single deity, and instead come to the Father as a child, aware that you come because of what the Son has done, helped by the Spirit who prays in you (Romans 8:26). Don't try to understand the Trinity this week. Pray to the triune God, and write down whether it changed the feel of your prayer.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God, we confess we've treated you as a riddle when you're our salvation. We're sorry for the years we defended you without worshiping you. We didn't invent you. You made yourself known, one God in three persons, and we receive that rather than vote on it. Thank you that you were never alone, that love isn't something you learned but something you've always been, and that you made us out of overflow and not need. Draw us, who are so often lonely, into the love you've had forever. We don't understand you. We adore you. Amen.
reflection: Have I treated the Trinity as a math problem or as the God I worship? What would it mean to receive it as a confession rather than a puzzle?
Which truth would I be tempted to drop to make God simpler, his oneness or the full deity of the Son and the Spirit, and what would I lose?
If God was never lonely and made me out of overflow, how does that change the way I come to him, and my fear that I have to keep him satisfied?
sessions.teaching:
We come to the Trinity as though we were walking up to a problem, and the problem looks like bad arithmetic. One God, three persons, and a voice in the back of the mind says that doesn't add up. So for most of us the Trinity becomes a doctrine we affirm and avoid, something we say in the creed and then set on a high shelf, true, we suppose, but not expected to do anything. My first question is whether the Trinity was ever a math problem at all, or whether we've been reading it as the wrong kind of thing.

The objection deserves to be heard at full strength. The charge is that the Trinity is incoherent, three gods smuggled in under one name, and worse, that it was invented: that the simple faith of Jesus, a Jewish teacher who believed in one God, was overgrown centuries later by councils that voted a complicated doctrine into being. Some of this is true, and granting it costs the answer nothing. The Trinity really can't be diagrammed. The three-leaf clover, water as ice and steam, the man who is a father and a son and a husband: press any of them and it turns into an error the church already named and rejected. If you've tried to draw the Trinity and failed, you haven't failed at faith. You've found out what the church already knew. And it's true that the precise vocabulary of one being and three persons was worked out later, at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and the Council of Constantinople in 381.

But watch what those councils actually did. They didn't invent the Trinity. They were driven to it by what they wouldn't surrender. Think of where the early church stood. Its first believers were Jews or taught by Jews, and the deepest confession of Israel was the Shema: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). There is one God. That wasn't negotiable. Yet those same believers found themselves doing what a strict monotheist should never do. They worshiped Jesus. He had said, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), taking the divine name on his own lips. He had forgiven sins, which everyone knew only God could do. He had received worship, which faithful people and angels in Scripture always refuse and turn back toward God (Acts 10:25-26; Revelation 22:8-9). And the church knew the Spirit not as an influence but as God present and personal. Jesus himself sent his disciples to baptize "in the name," singular, "of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19).

So they were held between two truths they couldn't drop: one God, and Jesus and the Spirit are that God. Most early errors were attempts to escape that tension by letting go of one side. In the early 300s, Arius taught that the Son was the highest created being but still a creature, which kept the arithmetic simple at the cost of Christ's deity. Nicaea met to reject that, confessing the Son "true God from true God," of one being with the Father. Others collapsed the three into one God wearing three masks. The councils weren't adding complexity for its own sake. They were drawing a fence. A creed is less a full description of God than a fence around him, ruling out what's false while leaving the mystery itself uncaptured. Augustine said in one of his sermons that if you've understood it, what you've understood isn't God.

The answer to the arithmetic is that God isn't three of the same thing he is one of. He's one in being and three in persons. Three gods would be a contradiction. One God who exists eternally as three persons is a mystery, which is a different thing: a truth too large for the container, not a falsehood too broken to hold.

It's possible to walk through all of that, the councils and the categories, and miss the point. So here's the heart of it. John writes that "God is love" (1 John 4:8). Not only that God loves, though he does, but that love is what he is. Now think about what love needs. It isn't something you can do alone. It gives itself to another and delights in another. If God were a single, solitary person, alone for all eternity before he made anything, there would have been no one for him to love, and love couldn't have been his nature. It would be something he started doing after he made someone to do it to. And a God like that would have made the world out of need, which would mean we exist to fill an empty place in God, loved the way a lonely man loves whoever finally walks into his empty house.

That isn't the God Scripture reveals, and the doctrine of the Trinity is why. The one God has existed forever as Father, Son and Spirit, in a communion of self-giving love, before a single star was made. Jesus speaks of the glory he had with the Father "before the world existed" and of the Father's love for him "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:5, 24). God was never alone. He was never short of love.

That's the least abstract truth there is. You weren't made by a lonely God scraping together someone to love. You were made out of overflow, by a love that was already complete and didn't need you, and made you anyway, to share what it already had. You aren't the cure for God's solitude. You're a guest invited to a feast that was already going. So the Trinity isn't the church's embarrassing math problem. It's the confession that the ground under everything isn't a force or a lonely will but a fellowship of Father, Son and Spirit who have loved each other forever and made a world to bring others in. We aren't here to solve it. We're here to be drawn into it.

scriptureStudy.note: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one." Israel's bedrock confession, which the church refused to give up. The Trinity is never three gods. It's always the one God of the Shema.

"Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." One name, singular, with three persons named within it, the oneness and threeness held together in a command of Jesus.

"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Word is with God, and so distinct, and is God, and so the same in being. The grammar of the Trinity is there in John's first sentence.
"Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am." Jesus takes the divine name on his lips and claims an existence that belongs to God alone. His hearers understood, and they picked up stones.
"I and the Father are one." Jesus claims a unity with the Father that is more than agreement, which the church later confessed at Nicaea as the Son being of one being with the Father.

"The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all." Paul blesses the church in the name of all three together, an early and unselfconscious witness to the triune shape of God.
"Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love." Love isn't only something God does but what he is, which can only be true of a God who was never alone.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at the work the church did to find words for the Trinity, because the precision was hard won and it matters. The crisis came in the early fourth century when Arius taught that the Son was the highest created being but still a creature, that "there was when he was not." The Council of Nicaea in 325 answered by confessing the Son "begotten, not made," homoousios, of one being with the Father. Athanasius, who spent much of his life defending that confession at great personal cost, argued in On the Incarnation that only God can save us, so that if the Son who saves us weren't truly God, we wouldn't really be saved. That's why the deity of Christ was never an abstract debate. Ask the group whether some truths are precise because they're important.

Then weigh Augustine's On the Trinity, written over about two decades, in which he holds both that the doctrine is true and that it goes beyond what we can fully grasp, so that the right response is worship rather than mastery. Notice too what the Eastern church especially kept in view: the persons of the Trinity dwell in one another in self-giving love, and to be saved is to be drawn into that communion (we'll come back to this in session 5). The discipline is to receive the doctrine as something confessed because it was revealed, not built because it was convenient, and to let careful language serve worship rather than replace it.

sessions.title: The Father Who Runs
sessions.aim: To meet the first person of the Trinity not as a distant lawgiver but as the father in Jesus's own parable, who runs toward the returning son, and to face plainly that for people whose fathers failed them "Father" may be the hardest word in the faith, without either a sentimental picture of God or the bitter conclusion that the word means nothing.
sessions.summary:
We've confessed the God who is three in one, and now we come to the first person of that fellowship, the Father. The moment we say the word, we hit something no doctrine can smooth over, because "Father" isn't a neutral word. What happens to someone whose father walked out, or never came, or stayed only to hurt them, when they're told to call God Father?

That wound is real, and for many in the room the word is a closed door, not an open arm. The gospel doesn't answer by throwing the word away, which would leave you praying to a force. Nor does it ask you to pretend your father was fine. It does something stranger. God isn't your father scaled up. He's the Father every earthly father was meant to reflect and fell short of. And Jesus shows us what he's like in a story: a father who sees his ruined son "while he was still a long way off," feels compassion, and runs (Luke 15:20).

Paul says that in Christ we've "received the Spirit of adoption as sons" (Romans 8:15). Adoption is for those who had no place. The first thing the gospel gives the fatherless isn't advice. It's a Father.

keyScripture.why: "And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). This is Jesus's own picture of the Father, who doesn't wait for the ruined son to grovel his way home but runs to meet him.

discussion.q: When you hear God called Father, what's your first, gut-level reaction, before the right answer? Where do you think it comes from?
discussion.behind: Bring out the gut response before you teach anything. For some the word is warm and for some it's a closed door, and the difference usually goes back to a human father. Don't try to settle it; just let it be named. Go first if the room is slow, and don't press anyone to explain.

discussion.q: What's the difference between thinking of God as a bigger version of your own father and thinking of him as the Father every human father was meant to reflect?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge for anyone who carries a wound here. Many quietly assume God is their earthly father scaled up, which is frightening for some. Help them feel the reversal: the human father is the imperfect copy, and God is the original, so the failures of one don't define the other. Handle it tenderly.

discussion.q: Read Luke 15:11-24. What surprises you about what the father does, and what he doesn't do?
discussion.behind: Point out what the father doesn't do: he doesn't wait, doesn't demand the speech, doesn't set conditions. He runs, embraces, kisses, and interrupts the apology with a robe and a ring. Many commentators note that a man of standing in that culture didn't run. Let the warmth of the scene correct the distant or punishing father many people fear God is.

discussion.q: Read Romans 8:15-17. Adoption means the right to call God Father is given, not earned. Where is it hardest for you to believe you're a child in his house and not a tolerated guest?
discussion.behind: Many believe in adoption as doctrine and live as orphans in practice, always trying to earn a place they've already been given. You're helping people see that gap, not fixing it.

discussion.q: Psalm 68:5 calls God "Father of the fatherless." What does it mean to you that God claims that title for himself?
discussion.behind: Let people sit with the fact that the title was aimed from the start at those who needed it most. Some may speak of their own fathers. Keep the room safe, don't let anyone be pushed to share, and check in privately afterward with anyone for whom this is fresh.

objections.objection: Calling God Father is fine for people who had good fathers. For the rest of us, it's cruel. You're asking me to feel safe with the very word that names the person who hurt me most, and no doctrine fixes that.
objections.response: That deserves to be heard, not managed. The word can land like a wound rather than a comfort, and pretending otherwise would be a lie. So hear the distinction carefully. Jesus isn't saying that God is a bigger version of your father. It's the other way around. God is the Father, the real one, and every earthly father, the absent one, the cruel one, and even the good one, was only ever a copy, and a broken one. Your father didn't define fatherhood for God to live up to. God defined it, and your father fell short. So when you call God Father, you aren't giving God the face of the man who failed you. You're appealing past that man to the One he was supposed to reflect and didn't. And look at what this Father is like. Jesus didn't describe a stern judge tapping his foot. He told about a father who saw his disgraced son a long way off and ran to him. The word belongs to that Father, not to your wound, and he's offering it to you.

objections.objection: If God is such a good Father, why did he let me grow up without one? You're offering me a heavenly Father as though that erases the human father I needed and never had. It doesn't. The hole is still there.
objections.response: The hole is real, and a heavenly Father doesn't give you back the childhood you should have had. So be clear about what the gospel claims and doesn't. It doesn't say the wound never happened or doesn't matter, and it doesn't promise that knowing God as Father makes the ache disappear. What it says is harder and truer. There was always supposed to be a Father. Your longing for one isn't a weakness. It's the right instinct, aimed at something real. The absence you grew up with was real, and it was wrong, and God doesn't bless it or excuse it. But the longing underneath it was pointing somewhere true the whole time. The gospel doesn't erase the empty chair. It tells you there's a Father who meant to fill it, who comes toward you now, and who will one day "wipe away every tear" (Revelation 21:4), that one included. The hole isn't denied. Slowly, it's met.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God is the Father your own father was meant to reflect, and he runs toward the returning child instead of waiting to be appeased, what's the one thing you've always needed a father to do or say that you've never had?
sessions.practice: This week, read the parable of the lost son in Luke 15:11-32 slowly each day, and each time stop at verse 20, where the father runs, and stay there. Don't hurry to the lesson. Picture yourself as the one coming home and God as the one running, and notice what rises in you, whether hope or disbelief or a flinch, without judging it. Then, once this week, call God Father out loud, even if the word is hard, and tell him plainly where it's difficult for you. If this stirs up more than you can carry alone, talk with your group leader, a pastor or a counselor you trust. Write down whether seeing God as the Father who runs changed how you came to him.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, some of us say that word easily, and some of us say it through clenched teeth, because the man it should have named left, or never came, or stayed and did damage. You know which of us is which. Thank you that you aren't an echo of our earthly fathers but the One they were meant to reflect, and that you aren't a judge waiting to be appeased but the Father who runs. To the fatherless among us, and there are more of us than we admit, give the news that they have a Father who has been coming toward them all the time they were sure no one would. Make us your children, not because we earned it, but because you ran. In the name of Jesus, your Son, who showed us your face. Amen.
reflection: What picture of a father do I bring to God without realizing it, and how has it shaped the way I relate to him, or kept me from him?
Where have I assumed God is my earthly father scaled up, when my earthly father was only ever a broken copy of him?
If I'm truly adopted, a child of God whether or not it feels true today, what would change about how I come to him this week?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent a session confessing the God who is three in one, and now we come to the first person of that fellowship, the Father. The moment we say the word, we run into something no doctrine can smooth over. "Father" isn't neutral. For some of you it's the warmest word there is, because behind it stands a man who was present and kind, strong and gentle in the right measure. For others it's a locked door. Behind it stands a man who left, or never appeared, or appeared only to wound, and being told to call God Father feels like being told to feel safe with the very name that taught you men can't be trusted to stay.

I was raised without a father, and I won't do what the church too often does, which is hurry past the wound to the comforting doctrine as though the pain were an interruption to the lesson. For many people it's the biggest obstacle between them and God, and it deserves to be named. So take the hardest form of the objection seriously. Calling God Father, it says, is a comfort if you had a good father and a cruelty if you didn't. You're asking the wounded to find safety in the word that names their deepest injury, and no theology repairs that.

I grant the weight of that. But it misses something, and getting the direction right is the turn of this whole session. Jesus isn't saying God is like your father. That's the fear that terrifies the wounded: that God is your earthly father scaled up, the same absence and the same temper with infinite power behind it. Jesus says the opposite. God is the Father, the original, and every human father who ever lived, the one who left, the one who stayed, even the rare good one, was a copy, and a broken one. Jesus argues this way himself: "If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him" (Matthew 7:11). Your father didn't set the standard that God then had to meet. God set it, and your father fell short. So when you call God Father, you aren't addressing the man who failed you with a bigger title. You're appealing past him to the One he was supposed to show you.

Then the question becomes what kind of Father the original is, and Jesus doesn't answer with a definition. He tells a story. A younger son asks for his share of the inheritance while his father is still alive, then goes to a far country and spends it all until he's starving and feeding pigs, about as low and unclean as the story could place a Jewish boy. He decides to go home, not hoping to be a son again, but only to be hired as a servant, and he rehearses his apology on the road: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son" (Luke 15:18-19).

Now listen to what the father does. "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). He'd been watching the road. Many commentators point out that a man of standing in that culture didn't run, that he'd have had to gather up his robes in front of the whole village. This father does it anyway, reaches his son before the speech is finished, and calls for the best robe, a ring and a feast. That's the Father the word belongs to. Not the judge with his arms crossed, waiting for the apology to reach the right pitch, but a Father who watches the road and runs. If your picture of God is a foot-tapping disciplinarian waiting to be appeased, Jesus is telling you, with this story, that you have the wrong father in mind.

What makes this yours and not just a moving story is a word Paul uses: adoption. Paul writes that "you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry" to God, Abba, Father (Romans 8:15). Adoption was a legal act, a deliberate decision to take someone who wasn't your child and make them your child, with the full standing and inheritance of one born into the house. And by definition it's for those who didn't have a father. You don't adopt your own children. You adopt the ones who had no place. God takes the fatherless and makes them sons and daughters, and gives them the right to call him not only Lord or Judge but Abba, the word a child uses at home. Long before Jesus, a psalm called God "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows" (Psalm 68:5). The title was always aimed at those who needed it most.

None of us teaches this from the far side of having it figured out. Many people come to God with no working picture of a good father and pray for years to a Father they can barely believe in, saying the word while some part of them braces for him to be like the absence they've known. Their adoption is true on those mornings whether or not it feels true. And slowly the running father of the story can overtake the absent father of their history, not by erasing the wound, but by being real and present and unlike the man they feared he'd be.

So the first thing the gospel gives the fatherless isn't a technique for healing or advice for coping. It's a Father. If you came tonight carrying an empty chair, hear this. There was always supposed to be a Father. The hunger you've carried isn't a defect. It's the shape of what you were made for, and it's being answered, not by a heavenly version of the man who failed you, but by the One he was meant to point you toward. Say the word, even if you have to say it like a child learning a name he never got to use. The Father is already running.

scriptureStudy.note: "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." Jesus's own picture of God the Father, who runs toward the returning son, the opposite of the distant or punishing father many fear.
"You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons." Paul says the Spirit himself prompts the cry of "Abba," Father, so even the word in our mouths is a gift and not an achievement.

"God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts," and the Spirit cries "Abba," Father. The closeness is the Spirit's work, which means the fatherless can call God Father truly, because God's Spirit, not our history, supplies the word.

"Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation." Long before Jesus, God claimed this title for those who had no father. It was always aimed at those who needed it most.

"See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are." Adoption isn't a thin metaphor. It's a real new standing, named by the Father over people who had none.

"If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him." Jesus argues from the broken copy to the original, from imperfect human fathers to a Father far better.
"Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." The Father isn't finally unknown. He has a face, the face of the Son, so the Father we're invited to call ours is the one we see in Jesus.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at the doctrine of adoption, because the modern habit of calling everyone a child of God in the same sense can empty the word of what makes it precious to the fatherless. The Reformers and the Puritans treated adoption as one of the high points of salvation. The sinner isn't only forgiven and acquitted, which is justification. The forgiven one is also brought into the family and given the standing of a son or daughter. J. I. Packer, in Knowing God, argues that adoption is the highest privilege the gospel offers, higher even than justification: to be justified is to be declared righteous by a judge, but to be adopted is to be received by a Father. Ask the group what is gained and what is lost when every person is simply assumed to be God's child in the same way.

Then weigh the pastoral edge. For those raised without a father, adoption isn't an abstraction. It's the very thing they most lacked and longed for, and the gospel offers it not as a consolation prize but at the center. Finally, set the father of Luke 15 beside every picture of God as a distant lawgiver who has to be appeased. Timothy Keller's The Prodigal God is a good guide to the parable. The discipline is to hold the word Father as both holy and tender, never so reverent it goes cold and never so familiar it goes cheap, remembering that for many in the room it's the most contested and the most longed-for word in the faith.

sessions.title: The Son Who Reveals
sessions.aim: To see that the God who could have stayed unknown made himself known in the Son, "the exact imprint of his nature," so that to see Jesus is to see the Father, and to hold the full deity and humanity of Christ as the church confesses them, against both reducing Jesus to a great teacher and turning God into an unknowable cloud.
sessions.summary:
Over this whole study hangs the oldest religious question there is: can God be known at all, or is he finally a cloud, a silence we project our guesses onto? The agnostic's position deserves respect. Every religion claims to know what God is like, they can't all be right, and the honest conclusion seems to be that the infinite is beyond us. If knowing God meant reasoning our way up to him, that would be the wise conclusion.

But the Christian claim isn't that we reasoned our way up. It's that God came down. Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Colossians calls him "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15). And when Philip asked Jesus to show them the Father, Jesus answered, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).

God didn't stay a cloud. He took a face, a voice, a pair of hands, and a way of treating lepers and children and a woman everyone else had condemned. If you want to know what God is like, you don't guess and you don't climb. You look at Jesus.

keyScripture.why: "He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power" (Hebrews 1:3). The Son isn't a messenger pointing toward a hidden God. He's the exact expression of God's own being, so in Jesus the invisible God has made himself truly visible.

discussion.q: Deep down, do you suspect God is finally unknowable, a mystery we can only guess at? Or do you believe he's made himself known? How does that shape your faith?
discussion.behind: Many believers carry a quiet agnosticism, a sense that God is ultimately a cloud we hope about. Name it without scolding it. The session will set it beside the claim that God has taken a face.

discussion.q: What's the difference between working out things about God by argument and being shown God in a person? Why might it matter which one Christianity claims to be?
discussion.behind: Help the room feel the difference between revelation and speculation. Most religious thinking climbs up toward God by reason. Christianity claims God came down. We aren't guessing about his character from a distance. We're reading it from an actual life.

discussion.q: Read John 14:8-9. If seeing Jesus is seeing the Father, then the way Jesus treated people is the way God treats people. Where does that differ from the God you've feared he might be?
discussion.behind: Many carry a picture of God as harsher than Jesus. Let the actual conduct of Jesus correct that picture: God is exactly as kind, and exactly as demanding, as Jesus was, and not secretly otherwise. Mention the leper he touched (Mark 1:41), the children he welcomed (Mark 10:14) and the woman he refused to condemn (John 8:11).

discussion.q: Many people admire Jesus as a wise teacher but stop short of calling him God. Why does the New Testament not let us stop there, and what would be lost if that were all he was?
discussion.behind: Hold the church's confession calmly and kindly. If Jesus is only a teacher, God remains unknown, because a teacher can describe God but can't be God made visible. And the Gospels show him forgiving sins, receiving worship and claiming to have existed before Abraham. Let people think it through rather than handing them the answer.

discussion.q: Are there ways you'd rather keep God vague? What does a God with a face ask of you that a cloud doesn't?
discussion.behind: Go first. A vague God makes no claim on anyone. A God with a face does. Revelation is a gift, and it's also a summons that's hard to dodge.

objections.objection: Every religion claims to know what God is like, and they all disagree. The honest position is that God, if there is one, is beyond all of us. Why should the Christian claim about Jesus be any different from anyone else's guess?
objections.response: That's the honest agnostic position, and it deserves respect. If knowing God meant reasoning our way up to the infinite, the humble conclusion would be that we can't, and our guesses would be only guesses. But the Christian claim isn't that kind of claim. It doesn't say we climbed up and figured God out. It says God came down and showed us. One is speculation about a distant object. The other is revelation by a personal God who chose to be seen. You don't reach the Christian picture of God by reasoning from the world to its cause and guessing at the character behind it. You reach it by looking at a particular man who lived at a particular time and did particular things, and hearing him say that to see him is to see the Father. That's a claim with a face and a record. You can read how he treated outcasts and children and the guilty and ask whether that's the character of God. You're free to reject that God came down. But it isn't the same kind of claim as a guess about a cloud.

objections.objection: I can admire Jesus as a great moral teacher, maybe the greatest, without believing he was God. Why isn't that enough? It looks like you're inflating a wise man into a deity to prop up a doctrine.
objections.response: It's a reasonable place to want to stop, and many sincere people do. But if Jesus was only a great teacher, God remains as unknown as before. A teacher can tell you things about God. He can't be God made visible, and the Christian claim isn't that Jesus described the Father well but that to see him is to see the Father. There's a harder problem too. The teacher said things no merely wise teacher would say. He forgave sins, which his hearers knew only God could do (Mark 2:5-7). He accepted worship. He said, "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58). A merely wise man who said those things wouldn't be wise. The calm, safe teacher-only Jesus isn't in the record. The church didn't inflate a wise man into God. It received a man who claimed to be God and was raised from the dead, and then spent centuries finding careful words for who he was. You can reject those claims. But the teacher-only Jesus is a figure we make by editing out what he said.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God isn't a cloud but has shown his face in Jesus, and the way Jesus treated the guilty and the outcast is the way God treats you, who have you been imagining God to be? Are you willing to let the real one replace the feared one?
sessions.practice: This week, read one of the Gospels, or a long stretch of one, with a single question in front of you: what is God like? Read it on the conviction that whatever Jesus is like, God is like. Watch how he treats the people everyone else wrote off: the leper he touched, the children he welcomed, the woman no one expected him to spare. Each time, instead of saying "that's how Jesus is," say "that's how God is." Write down where the God you saw in Jesus differed from the God you'd been quietly imagining, and what it would mean to trust the real one.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, some of us have spent our lives suspecting you were finally a cloud, a mystery we could only guess at, and keeping you vague because a vague God asks nothing of us. Thank you that you didn't stay hidden. You didn't leave us climbing and guessing. You came down and took a face, the face of Jesus, the radiance of your glory and the exact imprint of your nature, so we no longer have to wonder what you're like. Forgive us for preferring you abstract, and for fearing you were harsher than your Son. Teach us to see his kindness and his holiness as your own. Let us look at his face and find you there. In the name of the Son who showed us the Father. Amen.
reflection: Do I secretly believe God is finally unknowable? How would my faith change if I truly believed he has shown his face in Jesus?
Where is the God I fear harsher, colder or more distant than the Jesus of the Gospels, and what would it mean to let Jesus correct that picture?
What do I actually believe about who Jesus is, and have I let that be the ground of how I know the Father?
sessions.teaching:
We've met the Father who runs, and now a question hangs over this whole study that we need to face directly, because it's the oldest religious problem there is, and many believers carry a quiet version of it. Can God actually be known? Or is he finally a cloud, an infinite mystery, a silence onto which every religion projects its best guesses, so that all our confident statements about him are speculation dressed up as knowledge? This isn't only the skeptic's question. It lives in the church too, in the believer who affirms the doctrines but suspects underneath that God himself is out of reach, that we have words about him but not him.

The agnostic's position deserves more respect than the church usually gives it. Every religion claims to know what God is like, and they contradict each other. The god of one is wrathful, of another serene, of another many, of another a force. They can't all be right. So the humble conclusion seems to be that a being great enough to be God is greater than any human mind can map, and anyone who tells you confidently what God is like has mistaken a guess for knowledge. I grant the integrity of that. If knowing God means reasoning our way up to him, climbing from the world we can see toward an infinite we can't, then the cloud is too high and our best theology is only our best guessing. On that starting point, agnosticism isn't cowardice. It's honesty.

But the Christian claim isn't the kind the agnostic is rejecting. Christianity doesn't say we climbed up and figured God out. It says God came down. The letter to the Hebrews opens this way: "Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son" (Hebrews 1:1-2). Then it says of that Son, "He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature" (Hebrews 1:3). Radiance is to glory what light is to the sun, not a separate thing pointing back at it, but the shining of the source itself. And the word for "exact imprint" is the mark a seal leaves in wax, carrying every feature of the seal. The Son isn't a sketch of God or a messenger about God. He's the exact expression of God's own being. Paul says the same when he calls the Son "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), holding together two words that shouldn't fit: an image is something you can see, and invisible is what you can't.

John's Gospel puts it most plainly. On the last night, Philip says, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us" (John 14:8). He's asking the agnostic's question: just let us see God once, and we'll be satisfied. Jesus answers, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). You've been looking for God in the distance, he's saying, and God has been in front of you, eating with you, washing your feet, touching people no one touched.

That may be the most important claim in this study. God isn't finally unknown. The infinite didn't stay a cloud. He took a face and a voice and working hands and a particular way of moving through the world. So we have a way of knowing what God is like that isn't guessing and isn't climbing. We look at Jesus. And that's as concrete as anything can be, because it means the way Jesus treated people is the way God treats people. When a leper knelt in front of him, Jesus "stretched out his hand and touched him" (Mark 1:41), when a word alone would have healed him. When the disciples tried to send the children away, Jesus "was indignant" and said, "Let the children come to me" (Mark 10:14). When a woman caught in adultery was dragged before him by men ready to stone her, he said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more" (John 8:11), a mercy that didn't excuse the sin but refused the stone. If you've spent your life afraid that God is secretly harsher than Jesus, this takes that fear away at the root. Jesus isn't softening a hard God or standing in for a different one. There's no harsher God behind him.

There are two common ways out of this, and both are sincere. The first is to admire Jesus as a great moral teacher without believing he was God. It feels humble and reasonable. But if Jesus was only a teacher, God is as unknown as ever, because a teacher can tell you about God but can't be God made visible. And the teacher said things no merely wise man should say. He forgave sins, took the divine "I am" on his lips, and accepted worship. The calm, safe, teacher-only Jesus isn't in the record.

The second way out is to keep God abstract on purpose, and it tempts skeptics and believers alike, me included. Many of us want a God we can keep at a distance, because a God who is a cloud makes no demands. You can't disappoint a cloud. But a God with a face is harder to avoid. A God who looked at people and wept, who said "Follow me," has come close enough to ask something of you. Sometimes our deepest resistance to a knowable God isn't intellectual at all. It's that a known God is an unavoidable one.

So the agnostic is right that we can't climb up to God, and wrong that this leaves us in the dark, because God didn't wait for us to climb. "No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known" (John 1:18). The Son isn't a window onto a God who stays hidden behind the glass. He's God made visible, so that the most unknowable being there is became, in Jesus of Nazareth, a man whose words were recorded and whose face was turned toward the very people the world threw away. You don't have to guess what God is like. You can look at Jesus.

scriptureStudy.note: "He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature." The Son isn't a messenger about God but the exact expression of God's own being, so to see him is to see God truly, not approximately.
"He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation." Two words that shouldn't fit are held together: the invisible God is made visible in the Son.
"Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." Jesus answers the oldest religious longing, to see God, by saying that in seeing him the Father has already been seen.
"No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known." Revelation comes through the Son, not through our climbing up to God.
"And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory." The eternal Word took flesh, so God's glory wasn't glimpsed from afar but lived among us and was seen with human eyes.
"For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily." Not a portion of God or a representative of God, but the whole fullness of deity in the body of Jesus.
"Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am." Jesus claims an eternal existence that belongs to God alone, which a merely-great-teacher reading can't account for.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, take up the claim that only God can save, because it's why the deity of Christ was never an abstract debate. Athanasius, in On the Incarnation, argued that the human problem runs too deep for a creature to fix. What went wrong reached into death and corruption itself, so only the One who made us could remake us, only the author of life could defeat death from the inside. On his account the Son had to be truly God, because a created savior, however exalted, couldn't bridge the gap between God and us. That's why the Council of Nicaea in 325 fought so hard over a single word, confessing the Son to be of one being with the Father. Ask whether the difference between a Savior who is God and a Savior who is the greatest of creatures is the difference between a salvation that reaches all the way down and one that stops short.

Then look at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, which confessed Christ as one person in two natures, truly God and truly man. It guards both halves: the deity that makes God knowable in him, and the humanity by which he lived among us and showed us the Father in a human life. Read Hebrews 1 and Colossians 1 side by side and ask what kind of person these texts describe. The discipline is to hold the church's confession not as a doctrine to be defended in the abstract but as the ground of a very practical comfort: the face turned toward the leper and the child and the guilty is the face of God.
