sessions.title: The Spirit Who Indwells
sessions.aim: To end the study not with a diagram of God but with the life the Trinity makes possible: the Spirit who doesn't leave us studying God from across a room but draws us into the love the Father and the Son have shared forever, so that the doctrine becomes the shape of the Christian life rather than a truth admired from a distance.
sessions.summary:
We've confessed the God who is three in one and met the Father who runs and the Son who shows his face. Now we come to the person of the Trinity most often reduced to a vague force, the Spirit, and to the question the whole study has been moving toward. God has made himself known. Does he stay out there, someone we study, or does he come in?

It's true that the Spirit is the hardest person of the Trinity to picture. Scripture's images for him, wind and breath and fire, are forces, not faces. But Scripture speaks of the Spirit as a person. He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30). He gives gifts "as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11). And he isn't the distant one. He's the closest, God not only with us but in us. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed that "the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them" (John 17:26).

That's where the study ends. The point of the Trinity was never that you'd understand it. It was that you'd be brought inside it. Paul says that "God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" (Romans 5:5). You aren't a spectator of the love of God. You've been invited in.

keyScripture.why: "I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them" (John 17:26). Jesus prays that the eternal love between the Father and the Son would be in his people. This is where the doctrine of the Trinity has been heading: not a God studied from outside but a love we're drawn into.

discussion.q: Of the three persons, the Spirit is the one most of us know least what to do with. What has the Holy Spirit been to you, and why do you think he's the hardest to relate to?
discussion.behind: Many believers default to thinking of the Spirit as an "it," an energy, rather than a person. Name that habit gently. The session will recover the Spirit as the closest person of the Trinity, God not only with us but in us.

discussion.q: Looking back over the first four sessions, has this study been moving you toward understanding God better, being drawn closer to him, or both? What's the difference?
discussion.behind: Tie the study together. Session one said that knowing about God isn't the same as knowing him, and this is where that lands. Let people take stock without any pressure to report progress.

discussion.q: Read John 17:20-26. Jesus prays that the love the Father had for him "before the foundation of the world" would be in his people. What would it mean to believe that's true of you?
discussion.behind: We tend to hope God tolerates us. Jesus prays that we'd be loved with the love the Father has for the Son. Let that be as large as it is. It steadies people and humbles them at the same time.

discussion.q: Where do you relate to God like a spectator, watching from a distance? What would change if you believed the Spirit had actually brought you in?
discussion.behind: Many relate to God as someone admired from arm's length. The Spirit's work is to close that distance. Ask people to notice it, not to resolve it.

discussion.q: Is there a way you're still studying God from outside when you've been invited in? What keeps you in the doorway?
discussion.behind: Go first, briefly. It's possible to know this doctrine well and still stand outside the room it describes. End pointing into the room, not at the diagram.

objections.objection: The Spirit always sounds like the vaguest part of the Trinity, an impersonal force or energy, the leftover after the Father and the Son. Why should I relate to the Holy Spirit as a person at all rather than as God's power at work?
objections.response: That's a real difficulty. The Spirit is the hardest person of the Trinity to picture, partly because Scripture's images for him, wind, breath and fire, are forces, not faces. But Scripture consistently speaks of the Spirit as a person, not a power. He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), which an energy can't be. He teaches (John 14:26), intercedes (Romans 8:26) and gives gifts "as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11), which are the acts of someone with a mind and a will. Jesus called him "another Helper" (John 14:16), one who would be to his disciples what Jesus had been. And it matters a great deal. If the Spirit were only God's power, God would still relate to you from outside, acting on you like wind on a sail. But if the Spirit is God himself, then in the Spirit God comes to live in you. The Spirit isn't the abstract person of the Trinity. He's the nearest. To reduce him to a force is to keep God outside when he has come in.

objections.objection: This idea of being drawn into the love of the Trinity blurs the line between us and God, as if we become divine or get absorbed into God. That sounds more like Eastern mysticism than Christianity.
objections.response: That's a fair worry, and the line matters, so be clear about it. Being drawn into the love of the Trinity isn't being absorbed into God or becoming God. You remain a creature, fully yourself, distinct from your Creator. The goal isn't dissolving you into God but welcoming you, as you, into a fellowship of love. Think of the difference between a drop of water falling into the ocean and a guest welcomed into a family and given a seat at the table. The first loses the drop. The second keeps the guest and gives them a place. Jesus prays for the second in John 17: that the love between the Father and the Son would be in us, that we'd be brought into the fellowship, not melted into the substance. You don't become a fourth member of the Trinity. You're adopted, which is a relationship between distinct persons. The line between creature and Creator stands, and love crosses it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the point of the Trinity was never that you'd understand God but that you'd be brought into the love the Father and the Son have shared forever, are you still standing in the doorway? What's keeping you from stepping in?
sessions.practice: This week, end the study by living what it's been pointing toward. Each day, take a few minutes to do nothing but receive. Don't ask, study or perform. Sit with the truth that "God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Romans 5:5), that you aren't outside the fellowship of God looking in. When your mind reaches for something to understand or accomplish, set it down gently and come back. Pray to the Father, aware that you come through the Son and by the Spirit who lives in you. Write down what it was like to come to God not as a subject to master but as a fellowship that has welcomed you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, we've spent these weeks learning to say true things about you, and we're grateful. But the true things were never the point. You didn't make yourself known so we could pass a test about you. You did it so we could be brought into the love you've shared forever. Spirit of God, you aren't a vague force but God come to live in us, and you've poured into our hearts the love the Father has for the Son. Forgive us for standing in the doorway, studying the room we were invited into. Bring us in. Make what we've learned the shape of our days. We don't finally understand you. By your Spirit, we're coming to know you. Draw us all the way in. Amen.
reflection: Have I related to the Holy Spirit as a vague force or as the person of God who lives in me? What would change if I believed God had come not just beside me but into me?
If the love between the Father and the Son has been poured into my heart, why do I still relate to God as someone I have to keep satisfied?
After all this study, am I still a spectator of God? What would it mean to let the Spirit bring me in?
sessions.teaching:
We've confessed the God who is three in one, and we've met the Father who runs and the Son who shows us his face. Now we come to the third person, the one most of us know least what to do with. Ask a room of Christians to picture the Father and many will reach for the running father of the parable. Ask them to picture the Son and they'll see Jesus, with a face and a voice and a record of how he treated people. Ask them to picture the Holy Spirit and most of us go vague. We reach for an energy, a force, a feeling, a wind, something more like electricity than a person. The Spirit becomes the leftover of the Trinity, the one we affirm and aren't quite sure how to address.

And so the question this study has been circling comes due. God has made himself known. Does he stay out there, someone we study, however well? Or does he come in?

The difficulty is real. The Spirit is the hardest person of the Trinity to picture, not because anyone failed, but because Scripture's own images for him are forces: wind, breath, fire, a dove. None of them has eyes to meet. But Scripture speaks of the Spirit, consistently, as a person and not a power. Paul says, "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30), and you can't grieve an energy. The Spirit teaches (John 14:26), "intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26), and gives gifts "as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11). Those are the acts of someone with a mind and a will. On the last night Jesus said, "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth" (John 14:16-17), one who would be to the disciples what Jesus himself had been. And then he added, "You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you" (John 14:17).

That last phrase changes how we should think of him. The Spirit isn't the abstract person of the Trinity. He's the nearest. We could put it this way: the Father is God for us, the Son is God with us, and the Spirit is God in us. He closes the last distance. If you've thought of the Spirit as the vague one, you've had it backward.

Now we come to the words this study has been heading toward. They come from the longest recorded prayer of Jesus, in John 17, prayed the night before he died. He prays for his disciples, and then for everyone who would ever believe through their word (John 17:20), which means he prays for us. He asks "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us" (John 17:21). And he ends by asking "that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them" (John 17:26).

Think about the size of that. There's a love at the center of God that didn't begin when you were born or when the world was made, the love the Father has had for the Son "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). It's the same love we talked about in session two, the reason God can be called love at all. And the night before the cross, Jesus prayed that this love would be in us. Not that we'd watch it from the edge, but that it would be in us, so we're no longer outside the fellowship of God with our faces pressed to the glass, but brought in and given a place at the table.

That's the Spirit's work. "God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us" (Romans 5:5). The Spirit takes the love that has always flowed between the Father and the Son and pours it into us. He's the one who opens the door and brings us across the threshold.

So here's where the study ends, and it reaches back to where we began. In the first session I said there's a difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and that we'd study the highest doctrine the church holds not to win an argument but to be drawn into the God it describes. This is where that lands. The point of the Trinity was never that you'd understand it. I told you at the start you wouldn't be able to diagram it. The point was that you'd be brought inside it. The doctrine isn't a fence built to keep you on the road, studying the house from outside. It's the wall of a room you've been invited into.

I'll finish with a confession, because it's the danger of this whole study made personal. Those of us who teach can lay out Nicaea and Chalcedon, explain the radiance and the exact imprint, and show why God can be love only because he is three in one, and still, in a given week, relate to God as a subject we've mastered rather than a fellowship we've been welcomed into. We can stand in the doorway holding an excellent description of what's inside and never go in. So I'm speaking to myself first. Don't stop at the doorway. You didn't study the Trinity for five weeks to pass a test about God. You studied it so you'd know whose love you've been brought into: the love of a Father who runs, made visible in a Son who shows his face, poured into your heart by a Spirit who lives in you. That isn't a diagram. It's the shape of the Christian life.

scriptureStudy.note: "That the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them." Jesus prays that the eternal love between the Father and the Son would be in believers, the goal toward which the whole doctrine moves.

"That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us." The unity Jesus prays for is modeled on the unity of the Trinity, and it draws believers into that fellowship.
"God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." The Spirit pours the love of God into the believer, bringing the eternal love of the Trinity inside us.

"He will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth... he dwells with you and will be in you." Jesus speaks of the Spirit as a personal Helper who moves from being with the disciples to being in them.
"And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." Only a person can be grieved, not a force.
"All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills." The Spirit gives gifts as he chooses, the act of someone with a mind and a will.

"Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words." The Spirit within us prays for us, God at work in the believer's own heart.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at the old picture of the Christian life as sharing in the life of the Trinity, which is richer than reducing salvation to a transaction that gets us into heaven. Eastern Christian theologians spoke of the persons of the Trinity dwelling in one another in perfect self-giving love, each fully himself and fully open to the others, and they understood salvation as being drawn into that fellowship, not dissolved into God but welcomed into his life as creatures. Augustine, in On the Trinity, developed the idea that the Holy Spirit is in some sense the love shared between the Father and the Son, the bond of their fellowship. Set that beside Romans 5:5. If the Spirit is that bond of love, then to receive the Spirit is to receive into ourselves the love that unites the persons of God.

Ask the group whether their working picture of salvation is as large as John 17. When the goal of the faith shrinks to being forgiven and waiting for heaven, something is lost. And hold the line the tradition holds carefully: sharing in God isn't the creature dissolving into the Creator. It's the creature, still distinct and still itself, welcomed into the divine fellowship, a guest at the table and not a drop in the ocean. The discipline is to let the doctrine become the shape of an actual life, and to remember that all the long work of learning who God is was always an invitation to come in.

leaderPrimer:
The danger in leading this study isn't getting the doctrine wrong. It's getting it right. You're about to spend five weeks teaching the highest thing the church confesses, and it's entirely possible to finish with a group that can explain the Trinity and a leader who is better informed about God and no better acquainted with him. Session one names the difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and that distinction cuts toward the teacher first. You can explain Nicaea perfectly on a morning when God feels like a subject you've mastered rather than a Father you've come to. Take that as your assignment. Before each session, pray to the God the lesson describes, and if the prayer feels thinner than the preparation, say so in the room. Someone there has been quietly faking closeness to God for years and is waiting for a leader to go first.

Expect two kinds of difficulty, and don't confuse them. One is intellectual: the person who's sure the Trinity is a math problem Christians refuse to check. Session two will ease that, because the church never claimed to comprehend what it confesses. The other isn't intellectual at all. Session three takes up the word "Father," and for some people at your table that word is a wound with a name and a face. Say out loud that the word can be hard, and let those people breathe. Don't press anyone to talk about their own father. If someone is carrying something heavy, check in with them privately afterward, and help them find a pastor or counselor if they need more than the group can give.

Session four will bring up the quiet agnosticism many believers carry, the suspicion that God is finally a cloud and everyone is guessing. Don't correct it too fast. The faith doesn't ask anyone to climb up into the cloud. It announces that God came down and took a face. Every session ends in prayer rather than a summary, on purpose, because the doctrine was never the destination. Five weeks from now the question that matters is whether people stepped into the love the doctrine describes, or spent the whole study describing the room.

faq.q: Is this study going to be too intellectual, just abstract theology with no connection to my life?
faq.a: No. The whole study rests on the conviction that knowing about God and knowing him are different, and that theology that never becomes prayer has missed its purpose. Every session moves from the doctrine to the life it makes possible. The Trinity turns out to be the reason God can be called love. The fatherhood of God turns out to be good news for the fatherless. The deity of the Son means God isn't finally a cloud we guess at but a face we can see. And the Spirit is God come not only beside us but into us. If you came braced for a seminar, you'll find a study that treats the highest doctrine of the church as the shape of an ordinary Christian life.

faq.q: I find the Trinity confusing, and I'm not sure I understand it. Will the study expect me to?
faq.a: No, and that's by design. The church has never claimed to comprehend the Trinity, and every neat diagram of it turns out wrong. Augustine said in one of his sermons that if you've understood it, what you've understood isn't God. The councils of Nicaea and Constantinople didn't explain the mystery. They drew a fence around it, ruling out what's false without capturing the truth itself. So you won't be asked to solve the Trinity or draw it on a whiteboard. You're invited to receive it as the church has, as a confession of the God who saves us, and to be drawn into the love it describes. Confusion about the mechanics isn't failure here.

faq.q: Why spend a whole study on the Trinity? Isn't it an abstract doctrine that doesn't change anything?
faq.a: It changes more than almost anything, and session two makes the case. If God were a single, solitary person, alone before he made the world, then before there was anyone to love, God didn't love, because no one was there. Love would be something he took up after creation rather than something he is. But Scripture says "God is love" (1 John 4:8), and that can only be true if God was never alone, if within the one God there has always been a giving and receiving of love among Father, Son and Spirit. That means you weren't made by a lonely God who needed you, but out of a love that was already full. A solitary god would need you. The triune God can simply love you.

faq.q: I struggle to call God Father because of my own father. Is this study going to force that word on me?
faq.a: No, and session three is written with you in mind. It takes the wound seriously instead of waving it away. The key distinction is this: God isn't your earthly father scaled up. He's the Father every earthly father was meant to reflect and fell short of, so the failures of one don't define the other. And the session shows what this Father is like, not a stern judge waiting to be appeased but the father in Jesus's parable who saw his ruined son "while he was still a long way off" and ran (Luke 15:20). You're not disqualified by the wound. If the session stirs up more than the group can hold, talk with your leader, a pastor or a counselor you trust.

faq.q: Can't I just admire Jesus as a great moral teacher without all the talk of him being God?
faq.a: Many sincere people want to stop there, and session four explains why the New Testament doesn't let us. If Jesus was only a great teacher, God remains as unknown as before, because a teacher can tell you about God but can't be God made visible, and the Christian claim is that to see Jesus is to see the Father (John 14:9). And the teacher-only Jesus isn't really in the texts. The man in the Gospels forgave sins only God can forgive, accepted worship, and said, "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58). The church didn't inflate a teacher into God. It received a man who claimed to be God and was raised from the dead.

faq.q: Isn't it more honest to admit that God is finally unknowable, and everyone is guessing about his character?
faq.a: The study respects that position and agrees with part of it. If knowing God meant reasoning our way up to the infinite, the humble conclusion would be that we can't, and our guesses would be only guesses. But the Christian claim isn't that we climbed up and figured God out. It's that God came down and showed us, taking a face in Jesus. That's a different kind of claim, because it has a record you can read. You can look at how Jesus treated the leper, the child and the woman caught in adultery and ask whether that's the character of God. You're free to reject that God came down. But it isn't the same as a guess about a cloud.

faq.q: The Holy Spirit always seems like the vaguest part of the Trinity. Why should I relate to him as a person?
faq.a: Session five takes this up. The Spirit is the hardest person of the Trinity to picture, partly because Scripture's images for him, wind, breath and fire, are forces, not faces. But Scripture speaks of him as a person. He can be grieved (Ephesians 4:30), which an energy can't be. He teaches, intercedes and gives gifts "as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11). Jesus called him "another Helper" (John 14:16). And it matters, because if the Spirit were only God's power, God would still relate to you from outside. If the Spirit is God himself, then in him God comes to live in you. He isn't the abstract person of the Trinity. He's the nearest.

faq.q: Does being drawn into the love of the Trinity mean I get absorbed into God or become divine?
faq.a: No, and the study is careful here, because the line between creature and Creator matters. You remain a creature, fully yourself, distinct from your Maker. The goal isn't that you dissolve into God but that you're welcomed, as yourself, into a fellowship of love. Think of a guest welcomed into a family and given a seat at the table, not a drop of water lost in the ocean. In John 17 Jesus prays that the love between the Father and the Son would be in us, that we'd be brought into the fellowship, not melted into the substance. You don't become a fourth member of the Trinity. You're adopted, which is a relationship between distinct persons.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Why should I find the Christian God any more believable than any other claim about the divine?
faq.a: That's a fair challenge, and the study tries to answer it by refusing the easy version of faith. It doesn't claim we reasoned our way up to God and got him right, which is exactly the move a skeptic should be suspicious of. It claims that God came down and took a face in a particular man who lived at a particular time, whose words and conduct are on record. It also admits that many of us, believers included, prefer God abstract, because a vague God makes no demands. What the study offers isn't proof. It's a claim worth weighing: that in Jesus the unknowable God made himself known, and you can read what he was like and decide whether that's the face of God.

faq.q: Does this study assume I already have a strong faith, or is it for someone who feels distant from God?
faq.a: It's written for the person who feels distant, and it says so from the first session. The whole study is built to move people from knowing about God to knowing him, which assumes the gap is there. If you know the facts but not the Person, if God has felt more like a subject you study than a Father you come to, you aren't the exception. You're the person it was written for. The distance is treated as the place to start, not a failure to hide.

faq.q: Why does the study keep putting the writer and the leader inside the struggle instead of just teaching the doctrine?
faq.a: Because no one teaches this from the far side of having it all worked out. It's possible to defend the Trinity without worshiping the God being defended, and to stand in the doorway of the room these doctrines describe without going in. The writer and the leader are as prone to that as anyone. A leader who can say, "I struggle to know him too, not just to know about him," can sit beside the group as a fellow learner. Teaching from above tends to turn into either shame or distance. Teaching from alongside lets people stop pretending.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I find the Trinity hard to understand myself?
faq.a: That isn't a disqualification. The doctrine is hard, the church has always said so, and the study never asks anyone, leader included, to comprehend it, only to receive it and be drawn in. Every discussion question carries notes for the leader, every objection has a worked response, and every session ends in prayer, so you won't be improvising. Your own honesty about finding God hard to know may be the most freeing thing in the room. What you do need to do is refuse to make the Trinity a test, keep the room safe for the confused and the hurting, take special care in session three, and point everyone, yourself first, to the God who came down to be known.

timeline.event: Israel receives the Shema, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), the bedrock confession of one God that the church would never give up. The Trinity is never three gods but always the one God of Israel.

Jesus says "before Abraham was, I am," forgives sins only God can forgive, receives worship, and on the night before the cross prays in John 17 that the love the Father had for him before the foundation of the world would be in his followers.
Paul writes to the Romans that believers have received "the Spirit of adoption as sons" and that "God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (Romans 8:15; 5:5).

The letter to the Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature," and John's Gospel speaks of the Word who "was with God, and... was God." Hebrews is usually dated before John.

The Council of Nicaea answers Arius, who taught that the Son was the highest creature but still a creature, and confesses the Son "begotten, not made," of one being with the Father, true God from true God.

Athanasius writes On the Incarnation (its exact date is debated), arguing that only God can save, so that if the Son who saves us were not truly God we would not really be saved. He spends much of his life defending the Nicene confession at great personal cost.
The Council of Constantinople expands the Nicene Creed to confess the Holy Spirit as "the Lord and giver of life," worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son.

Augustine writes the Confessions, which opens by saying our heart is restless until it rests in God, and then spends about two decades on On the Trinity, holding that the doctrine is true and that it goes beyond our full understanding.
The Council of Chalcedon confesses Jesus Christ as one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion or division.
John Calvin publishes and revises his Institutes. In the 1559 edition (1.2.1) he says God isn't properly known where there is no piety, which he defines as reverence joined with love of God.

Karl Barth publishes the first volume of his Church Dogmatics, placing God's self-revelation in Christ at the center of theology: God is known because he has made himself known, not because we reasoned our way up to him.
J. I. Packer publishes Knowing God, built on the difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and arguing that adoption is the highest privilege the gospel offers.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. Talking honestly about God, the real one and not the one we're supposed to perform for, is harder than it sounds. A few things before we start. First, this is a safe room. You can say here that the Trinity makes no sense to you, or that God feels like a force more than a person, or that the word Father is hard for you, or that you're not sure God can be known. Nobody will grade you or hand you a quick fix. Second, this study isn't a test you pass by understanding the doctrine. The church has never claimed to fully understand the Trinity, and we won't pretend to either. We're after something else: moving from knowing about God to knowing him. Third, I'm in this with you. I've known a lot about God on mornings when he felt far away. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this passage says about who God is. Now let's bring it home, into the week ahead, the ordinary mornings and the hard nights where we either come to this God or keep him at a distance. That's where this matters or doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: Let's stop there. If it doesn't feel finished, that's all right. Knowing God isn't something we complete on a schedule. Take this into your week. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions. If the word Father is hard for you, or you suspect God can't really be known, or you've realized you've been studying God more than coming to him, please don't carry it alone. Talk to me, or to someone you trust in this room. Let me pray for us before we go, because this study ends each week not in a summary but by coming to the God we've been studying.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and shame, and name plainly that the goal is not to understand the Trinity but to come to know the God it describes, and that for some the word Father is a wound and this room is safe for that.
Week 2: Session 1, Knowing vs. Knowing About, full discussion and practice, with extended time on the gap between knowing facts about God and actually meeting him.
Week 3: Session 2, part one, One God, Three Persons, the doctrine stated carefully and historically, Nicaea and Chalcedon, the fence around the mystery rather than a solution to it.
Week 4: Session 2 continued, the heart of it, that God can be love only because he was never alone, and what it means to be made out of overflow rather than need.
Week 5: Session 3, The Father Who Runs, the fatherhood of God and the parable of the prodigal, handled with great care for those whose earthly fathers failed them.
Week 6: Session 4, The Son Who Reveals, the deity of Christ and the claim that God is not finally a cloud but has shown his face, with time for the doubting and the agnostic.
Week 7: Session 5, The Spirit Who Indwells, God in us and the love of the Trinity poured into the heart, the doctrine as the shape of the Christian life.

Week 8: Integration. Pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, together, revisit the five practices, and name where each person has moved from studying God to coming to know him, with space for anyone needing further help.

bibliography.title: Knowing God
bibliography.author: J. I. Packer
bibliography.note: Published in 1973. Built on the difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and the source of the argument that adoption is the highest privilege the gospel offers. Useful for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: On the Incarnation
bibliography.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
bibliography.note: Argues that only God can save, so that if the Son were not truly God we would not really be saved. Background for sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: On the Trinity
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Augustine's long treatment of the doctrine, written over about two decades. It holds both that the Trinity is true and that it exceeds our understanding, and it develops the idea of the Spirit as the love between the Father and the Son. Background for sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Opens with the line that our heart is restless until it rests in God. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: The Institutes of the Christian Religion
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: In the 1559 edition (1.2.1), Calvin ties true knowledge of God to piety, reverence joined with love. Supports session 1.

bibliography.title: Delighting in the Trinity: An Introduction to the Christian Faith
bibliography.author: Michael Reeves
bibliography.note: A warm, readable case that the Trinity isn't an awkward add-on but the reason God is love and the gospel is good news. A good companion to session 2.

bibliography.title: The Prodigal God: Recovering the Heart of the Christian Faith
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A close reading of the parable in Luke 15, including the father who runs. A good companion to session 3.

bibliography.title: The Pleasures of God: Meditations on God's Delight in Being God
bibliography.author: John Piper
bibliography.note: On the Father's delight in the Son as the ground of God's joy and of his love for us. Background for session 5.

bibliography.title: Church Dogmatics
bibliography.author: Karl Barth
bibliography.note: A massive work, begun in 1932, that places God's self-revelation at the center of theology. Background for session 4's account of the Son who makes the Father known.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On the tender heart of Christ toward the weary. Helpful for those who find the word Father hard and need to see God's heart in the face of the Son, in sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: A Secular Age
bibliography.author: Charles Taylor
bibliography.note: Describes the modern "buffered self," sealed off from any sense of the transcendent. Helps explain the quiet agnosticism and the preference for an abstract God that session 4 takes up.

bibliography.title: The Holy Trinity: In Scripture, History, Theology, and Worship
bibliography.author: Robert Letham
bibliography.note: A thorough account of the doctrine's biblical roots and historical development, including Nicaea, Constantinople and Chalcedon. A reference for leaders who want depth behind session 2.

furtherReading: Knowing God, J. I. Packer, for anyone who wants to stay longer with the difference between knowing about God and knowing him.
Delighting in the Trinity, Michael Reeves, for those who want to see why the Trinity is good news and the reason God is love, alongside session 2.
The Prodigal God, Timothy Keller, for anyone who needs the running father of the parable, especially those for whom the word Father is hard, alongside session 3.
On the Incarnation, Athanasius, for the ancient argument that only God can save, alongside session 4.
The Confessions, Augustine, for those who want to walk with a restless heart that finally came to rest in God.

glossary.definition: The Christian confession that the one God exists eternally as three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one in being and three in persons. This study treats it not as a puzzle to solve but as the reason God can be called love.
Personal acquaintance with God himself, as distinct from knowing about God, which is gathering true facts about him. On this study's account, the first is the aim of all theology.

The distinction that keeps the Trinity from being a contradiction: God is one in being (one "what") and three in persons (three "whos"). Three gods would be a contradiction. One God in three persons is a mystery, a truth too large for the container.
The council that answered Arius and confessed the Son "begotten, not made," of one being with the Father, true God from true God, ruling out a Christ who is merely the highest creature.
The council that confessed Jesus Christ as one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion or division.

God's act of making those who weren't his children into sons and daughters, with the right to call him Father. Packer called it the highest privilege the gospel offers, and it is given, by definition, to those who had no place.

The Aramaic word for father that Jesus used in prayer (Mark 14:36), and that the Spirit prompts in God's adopted children (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). It's the word a child uses at home, given by grace rather than earned.
The phrase in Hebrews 1:3 for the Son. The Greek word was used for the mark a seal or stamp leaves, carrying every feature of the original, so that to see Jesus is to see the Father truly.

Paul's phrase in Colossians 1:15 for the Son. It holds together two words that shouldn't fit, image (something seen) and invisible (something unseen): the God no one can see has been made visible in Jesus.
God making himself known by coming to us, as distinct from speculation, our reasoning up toward a distant God. The Christian claim is that we didn't climb to God; God showed his face in the Son.
The truth that the Holy Spirit, a person and not a force, comes to live in the believer, so God isn't only above us and beside us but in us.

Being drawn by the Spirit into the love the Father and the Son have always shared, as a welcomed guest and not an absorbed drop. The creature remains distinct from the Creator while being brought into his fellowship.

Augustine's account of sin as loving lesser things more than greater ones, putting created goods where only the Creator belongs. It stands behind his conviction that the heart is restless until it rests in God.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Many of us have studied God for years and quietly suspect we've never met him. This five-session study walks through the oldest confession the church holds, that the one God is eternally Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and asks whether the point was ever only to be right about God, or to know him. It moves from knowing about God to knowing him, through the Trinity as the reason God can be called love, the Father who runs toward the returning child, the Son in whom God took a face, and the Spirit who draws us into the love at the center of God. It's gentle with those for whom the word Father is hard, and it never makes the Trinity a test. Any volunteer can lead it with no preparation.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on knowing God, walking through the doctrine of the Trinity. Before anyone braces for abstract theology: this study won't grade whether you understand the Trinity, because the church has never claimed to fully understand it either. It's about moving from knowing about God to actually knowing him, and it takes the hard parts seriously: the word Father when your own father failed you, the suspicion that God can't really be known, the gap between studying God and meeting him. I need it as much as anyone. There's no homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: We can know a great deal about God and never have met him. A five-session study on the Trinity: the God who is love because he was never alone, the Father who runs, the Son who took a face, and the Spirit who brings us in. Gentle with those for whom the word Father is hard, and it never makes the Trinity a test.
quoteCards: You can know that God is good and never once have rested in it. Theology that never becomes prayer has missed its own point.
God isn't your father scaled up. He's the Father every father was meant to reflect.
A solitary god would need you. The triune God can simply love you, because he was never short of love.
You weren't made by a lonely God who needed someone. You were made out of a love that was already full.
The father didn't wait at a distance to be appeased. He saw his son a long way off, and he ran.
God isn't finally a cloud. He took a face. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus.
The Spirit isn't the vague person of the Trinity. He's the nearest: God not only with us but in us.
The point of the Trinity was never that you'd understand it. It was that you'd be brought inside it.
